# Setup

`BiocManager` is recommended for installing the packages required in this
vignette.
`BiocManager` handles installation from Bioconductor, CRAN and GitHub
repositories.

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!"BiocManager" %in% rownames(installed.packages()))
    install.packages("BiocManager")
pkgs <- c(
    "spliceTerrain", "RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14", "EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75",
    "AnnotationFilter", "ensembldb", "GenomicRanges", "scales", "pander",
    "GenomeInfoDb"
)
BiocManager::install(pkgs, update = FALSE)
```

Now we can load the packages used below.

```{r pkgs}
library(spliceTerrain)
library(RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14)
library(EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75)
library(AnnotationFilter)
library(ensembldb)
library(GenomicRanges)
library(scales)
library(pander)
library(GenomeInfoDb)
```

# Quick start

At a minimum, `spliceTerrain()` needs BAM file paths and a genomic interval.
Here we use BAM files from `RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14`, selecting one HNRNPC
knockdown sample and one control sample.
The region can be supplied as a single character string.

```{r quickstart, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
bams <- RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14_BAMFILES[c(7, 1)]
region <- "chr14:70,233,810-70,238,690"

spliceTerrain(bam = bams, region = region)
```

# Introduction

Sashimi plots visualise RNA-seq alignments across a genomic interval.
They combine coverage tracks with arcs representing splice junction support.
`spliceTerrain` reports both coverage and junction support in fragment units.
This makes them useful for inspecting transcript structure, exon usage,
alternative splice sites, intron retention, and differences in junction usage
between samples.

## Motivation

`spliceTerrain` was designed to fit into R/Bioconductor workflows.
Candidate regions, exon models, and features of interest are often already
represented as `GRanges` or `GRangesList` objects.
Reuse these objects for regions, transcript annotation, and highlights
alongside indexed BAM files, within the same R session.
For example, exon models retrieved from an `EnsDb` can become annotation rows
without first exporting them to an annotation file.

`spliceTerrain` brings these inputs together in a focused, sample-resolved
sashimi workflow.
It returns a `patchwork` plot or an inspectable genomic context.
Its genomic summaries and plotting settings can be edited and replotted.

## Related tools and positioning

[Gviz][gviz-package] [@Hahne2016], [ggbio][ggbio-package] [@Yin2012], and
[ggsashimi][ggsashimi-package] [@GarridoMartin2018]
provide established approaches to related visualization tasks.

| Tool | Documented focus | Interface |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Gviz | Genomic tracks, coverage and sashimi | R/grid track objects |
| ggbio | Genomic graphics and splice summaries | R/ggplot2-based graphics |
| ggsashimi | Sashimi, overlays and sample aggregation | Python/R command line |

Gviz supports BAM-backed alignment tracks, annotation tracks, junction filters,
and user-supplied junction summaries.
ggbio supports Bioconductor objects, editable graphics, track composition, and
gap truncation.
Its `plotSpliceSum()` function summarises support against transcript models,
with optional weighting of reads matching multiple models.
ggsashimi supports optional annotation, junction-derived shrinking, sample
overlays, and mean/median aggregation, and can export junction BED files or
generate an R script for subsequent use.
R integration, editable graphics, and gap compression are therefore shared
capabilities; spliceTerrain's emphasis is their combination with the following
specific choices:

- **An inspectable genomic context.** `return_ctx = TRUE` exposes genomic
    `GRanges` summaries and settings, and `ctx` rebuilds the figure from them.
    This supports iterative filtering and annotation changes with range
    operations, followed by remapping and plotting without another BAM import.
    Gviz also caches regional data and ggbio provides reusable plot objects;
    spliceTerrain exposes its processed genomic summaries as a flat context.
- **A shared, feature-preserving map.** Compression uses retained coverage from
    all samples, supplied annotation, and junction/selection anchors to define
    blocks whose widths are preserved; gaps receive a chosen plot-space width.
    A retained covered segment inside an annotated intron can remain visible
    at its original width, even without an annotated exon there.
    This differs from ggsashimi's junction-derived, length-dependent shrinking.
    The coverage thresholds determine which signal contributes to the map.
- **Explicit counting and usage semantics.** Coverage and junction support use
    fragments, including mapped singletons; overlapping mates count once per
    covered base and once per distinct junction.
    In the reviewed default Gviz alignment-track and ggsashimi counting paths,
    both mates can contribute read-level support.
    Local junction usage uses an unfiltered reference, so hiding an arc does
    not change another arc's percentage.
- **Annotation as an overlay on observed signal.** Transcript models are
    supplied as a `GRangesList`; metadata controls feature colours and labels.
    `annotated_junctions` distinguishes matching and unmatched junctions
    relative to those models, while retaining the underlying fragment counts.
    This is complementary to ggbio's model-based `plotSpliceSum()` workflow.
    Arc placement, height, width scaling, and panel proportions are explicit
    plotting controls.
- **Sample-specific controls in one call.** Library sizes and normalisation
    factors, per-BAM strand modes and thresholds, and a common y-axis option
    support comparisons while the samples share one coordinate map.

The examples below demonstrate this combination with
[transcript annotation](#adding-transcript-annotation),
[compressed layouts](#compressed-genomic-layouts),
[local junction usage](#local-junction-usage-labels), and
[context reuse](#returning-and-reusing-plot-data).
The intended task is visual inspection of candidate splicing differences at a
locus across selected samples.
Gviz and ggbio offer broader genomic visualization frameworks, while ggsashimi
provides a file-driven command-line workflow and sample aggregation.
spliceTerrain uses one panel per BAM and does not perform differential-splicing
tests, event-level PSI estimation, or transcript-isoform inference.

This comparison was checked on 13 October 2026 against the documented workflows
and source of Gviz 1.57.4 and ggbio 1.61.0 (Bioconductor 3.24 devel), and
ggsashimi 1.1.5.
The reviewed source snapshots are available for [Gviz][gviz-source],
[ggbio][ggbio-source], and [ggsashimi][ggsashimi-source].
The comparison concerns those workflows and defaults, rather than what could
be achieved by supplying custom importers, summaries, or plotting code.

[gviz-package]: https://bioconductor.org/packages/Gviz/
[ggbio-package]: https://bioconductor.org/packages/ggbio/
[ggsashimi-package]: https://github.com/guigolab/ggsashimi
[gviz-source]: https://github.com/ivanek/Gviz/tree/482799c06b17
[ggbio-source]: https://github.com/bioconductor-source/ggbio/tree/5d6ed36bdeb6
[ggsashimi-source]: https://github.com/guigolab/ggsashimi/tree/v1.1.5

# Complete guide

The following sections build up aspects of a more complete plot and introduce
the main options available in `spliceTerrain()`.
The examples continue to use the HNRNPC chr14 BAM files from the quick start.

## Input BAM files and regions

The `bam` argument is a character vector of indexed BAM file paths.
If the vector is named, those names are used as sample labels in the plot.
If it is unnamed, labels are derived from the BAM file names.
BAM files must be indexed for region-restricted import.
Index files should be discoverable by `Rsamtools` using standard same-directory
naming, typically `file.bam.bai`.

```{r named_bams}
bams <- RNAseqData.HNRNPC.bam.chr14_BAMFILES[c(7, 1)]
names(bams) <- c("HNRNPC knockdown", "Control")
```

The `region` argument can be a character string, a `GRanges`, or a
`GRangesList`.
Character regions may use comma-separated coordinates, such as
`"chr14:70,233,810-70,238,690"`.
For Bioconductor workflows, using a `GRanges` object is often more convenient.

Because the example BAM files use UCSC style chromosome names, we also convert
the region to UCSC style before plotting.

```{r region}
ensDb <- EnsDb.Hsapiens.v75
region <- transcripts(ensDb, filter = TxIdFilter("ENST00000394366"))
seqlevelsStyle(region) <- "UCSC"
region
```

If multiple ranges are supplied, `spliceTerrain()` reduces them to a single span
on one chromosome and uses that span as the BAM query and plotting window.
The span is the smallest continuous interval containing all supplied ranges: it
starts at the lowest start coordinate and ends at the highest end coordinate.

## Adding transcript annotation

Transcript models can be displayed with the `annotation` argument.
This must be a `GRangesList`, where each list element represents one transcript
or feature group.
The names of the list elements are used as y-axis labels in the annotation
panel.
When annotation is present, the final plot contains one panel per BAM file plus
one annotation panel.
The relative heights of these panels are controlled with `panel_heights`, where
the final value corresponds to the annotation panel.
Setting `annotated_junctions = TRUE` distinguishes junctions that exactly match
an intron in the supplied annotation with solid arcs, while unmatched junctions
are drawn with dashed arcs.
Junction classification is relative to the supplied annotation, so known
junctions may appear unmatched when only a subset of transcripts is provided.

For this vignette, the plotting region covers the *SRSF5* gene.
We retrieve exon ranges for the gene and keep a small number of transcripts so
the annotation panel remains readable.

```{r annotation}
annotation <- exonsBy(
    ensDb, by = "tx", filter = GeneIdFilter("ENSG00000100650")
)
annotation <- annotation[1:3]
seqlevelsStyle(annotation) <- "UCSC"
```

```{r annotation_plot, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=7.5}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    annotation = annotation,
    annotated_junctions = TRUE,
    panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1)
)
```

## Styling annotation tracks

Annotation features can be coloured by a metadata column with `anno_fill_by`.
Use `"group"` to colour each transcript or feature group separately.
Specific fill colours can be supplied with `anno_fill_colours`.

Text labels can be drawn inside annotation features with `anno_label_by`.
The label colour and size are controlled by `anno_label_colour` and
`anno_label_size`.
The `min_arrow` argument controls how wide an annotation intron must be before
directional arrows are drawn.

```{r annotation_styling, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=7.5}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    annotation = annotation,
    panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1),
    anno_fill_by = "group",
    anno_fill_colours = c(
        ENST00000553369 = "#66C2A5",
        ENST00000394366 = "#8DA0CB",
        ENST00000451983 = "#FC8D62"
    ),
    anno_label_by = "exon_rank",
    anno_label_colour = "black",
    anno_label_size = 2.5,
    min_arrow = 100
)
```

## Highlighting regions of interest

The `highlight` argument marks one or more genomic intervals with shaded
vertical bands.
This is useful for drawing attention to a splice site, variant position,
alternative exon, or other feature of interest.
The highlighted interval can be supplied as a character string or as a
`GRanges` object.

```{r highlight_site, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    highlight = "chr14:70234854-70234854",
    highlight_colour = "red"
)
```

A wider interval can be highlighted with a semi-transparent colour.

```{r highlight_exon, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    highlight = "chr14:70234056-70234097",
    highlight_colour = scales::alpha("red", 0.2)
)
```

## Local junction-usage labels

The `junction_usage` argument selects junctions by a genomic position or range
and labels their relative fragment support within each sample.
Junctions are selected when either their start or end anchor overlaps the
supplied interval(s).
Junction anchors use intronic coordinates: the start anchor is the first base of
the intron, and the end anchor is the last base of the intron, not the adjacent
exonic bases.

**Selecting a single shared splice site gives the cleanest interpretation.**
For junctions sharing a donor or acceptor, the labels describe their relative
support at that site.
By default, the junction count and usage percentage are separated by a new line.
Use `junction_usage_label_sep = " "` to display them together on one line.

```{r junction_usage_site, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    junction_usage = "chr14:70234854-70234854",
    junction_usage_label_sep = " "
)
```

A range can also be supplied, including one covering multiple splice sites.
It defines a combined set of selected junctions; each junction enters the
denominator once, even if both anchors or overlapping intervals select it.

```{r junction_usage_range, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    junction_usage = "chr14:70234098-70234854"
)
```

For each sample, the percentage is the junction's raw fragment support divided
by the summed support of all selected, eligible imported junctions.
This is calculated after import, MAPQ, and strand filtering, but before
`min_junction_reads` filtering or plotting-window exclusion.
An alternative junction remains in the denominator when its arc is hidden.
For example, supports of 90 and 9 give 90.9% and 9.1%; hiding the second arc
with a threshold of 10 leaves the first label at 90.9%, not 100%.
Visible percentages therefore need not sum to 100%.
Library-size normalisation and intron compression do not change the fractions.
Labels are rounded to one decimal place, and no percentage is shown when the
selected support is zero.
The reference is conditional on the imported data: changing the query region,
MAPQ threshold, or strand selection can change the available evidence.

### Why this is not event-level PSI

Consider a cassette exon between an upstream and a downstream exon.
In a simplified example, 50 inclusion fragments support both inclusion
junctions, and 50 skipping fragments support the direct skipping junction.
A range selecting all three junctions gives the following junction-usage labels:

```{r cassette_usage_example}
cassette <- data.frame(
    Junction = c("Upstream inclusion", "Downstream inclusion", "Skipping"),
    Fragments = c(50L, 50L, 50L)
)
cassette[["Junction usage (%)"]] <- round(
    100 * cassette$Fragments / sum(cassette$Fragments), 1
)
pander(cassette)
```

The denominator is 150 units of junction support, so each label is 33.3%.
There are only 100 fragments in this constructed example, with a known exon
inclusion fraction of 50%: each inclusion fragment supports two junctions.
Thus the 33.3% labels are not estimates of the cassette exon's inclusion.
Selecting one shared donor or acceptor instead compares one inclusion junction
with the skipping junction and gives 50% for each in this example.
Ranges remain useful for inspecting broader patterns, but their combined
junction fractions should not be interpreted as general event-level
percent spliced in (PSI) or transcript-isoform proportions.

## Filtering signal

Three arguments control how much signal is imported and displayed.
`min_mapq` filters alignments by mapping quality during BAM import.
`min_coverage` filters positions by per-base fragment coverage before plotting.
Despite its name, `min_junction_reads` filters splice junction arcs by their
supporting fragment count.
Both mates supporting the same junction contribute one count.
The latter two arguments also accept percentage strings such as `"10%"`.
Percentage thresholds are calculated separately for each BAM relative to its
maximum raw coverage or junction count within the plotting region.
When supplying one threshold per BAM, whole-number counts and percentages can be
mixed in a character vector.

```{r filtering, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    min_mapq = 10,
    min_coverage = 10,
    min_junction_reads = "10%"
)
```

Technical note: `min_coverage` and `min_junction_reads` are applied to raw
counts before any library-size normalisation is applied.

## Stranded RNA-seq data

The `strandedness` argument describes how read strand should be interpreted.
It can be one of `"unstranded"`, `"forward"`, or `"reverse"`, and can be
supplied either as a single value for all BAM files or one value per BAM file.
The example BAM files are unstranded, so both read orientations contain signal
from the transcript.

```{r strandedness, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    strandedness = "unstranded"
)
```

Specifying a stranded protocol for unstranded BAM files filters reads by strand.
As a result, either `"reverse"` or `"forward"` shows only part of the coverage
that is visible when `strandedness = "unstranded"`.

```{r forward_strandedness, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    strandedness = "forward"
)
```

```{r reverse_strandedness, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    strandedness = "reverse"
)
```

For paired-end BAM files, `spliceTerrain()` detects paired-end status from the
BAM alignment flags and imports alignments accordingly.
Mapped reads are retained even when their mates are unmapped.
Read-one/read-two flags determine strand interpretation for both complete pairs
and singletons.
Unmapped, secondary, supplementary, and below-`min_mapq` alignments are
excluded.
If `region` specifies a strand and `strandedness` is not `"unstranded"`,
alignments are restricted to the resolved region strand.

Coverage and junction support are fragment-level summaries.
Each imported mate group, mapped singleton, or single-end read is one fragment.
Coverage uses the union of each fragment's aligned blocks.
Overlapping mates contribute at most one count per covered position.
Introns and unsequenced gaps between mates remain uncovered.
Each fragment supports a distinct junction at most once, even if both mates
cross it; the same fragment can support multiple different junctions.
Independent fragments with identical coordinates still count separately.
This is not PCR/UMI deduplication.
Keeping mapped singletons avoids discarding their signal when mate-mapping
success differs between samples.

## Normalising between samples

When samples have different sequencing depths, coverage and junction counts can
be normalised with `lib_size`.
Supply full-library sizes in fragment units before restriction to the plotting
region: one per pair or mapped singleton, or one per read for single-end data.
Additional normalisation factors, such as `edgeR` TMM factors, can be supplied
with `norm_factors`.
The effective library size is calculated as `lib_size * norm_factors`.

By default, counts are normalised to the median effective library size.
Use `normalise_to` to set the target explicitly.
The `common_y` argument is useful when comparing samples because it puts sample
panels on the same y-axis scale.

```{r normalisation, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    lib_size = c(40e6, 55e6),
    norm_factors = c(0.95, 1.08),
    normalise_to = 50e6,
    common_y = TRUE
)
```

## Compressed genomic layouts

By default, `compress_introns = TRUE` compacts large uninformative gaps so the
plot focuses on observed signal.
The `intron_width` argument controls the approximate width of compacted introns
in plot space.
The map is built jointly from retained coverage across samples, annotations,
and junction/selection anchors.
Retained blocks keep their widths; gaps between them receive the chosen width.
Consequently, retained intronic coverage or an unannotated covered exon remains
part of the displayed signal rather than being compressed simply because it lies
inside an annotated intron.
Changing coverage filters can change the retained blocks and their map.

```{r compress_introns, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    compress_introns = TRUE,
    intron_width = 500
)
```

If exact genomic distances are more important than compact display, intron
compression can be disabled.

```{r no_compression, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    compress_introns = FALSE
)
```

## Junction arc display

Junction arcs can be tuned with `arc_height`, `arc_side`, and `arc_scale`.
Increasing `arc_height` gives stacked arcs more vertical separation.
The `arc_side` argument controls whether arcs are drawn above, below, or on both
sides of the coverage track.
With `arc_scale = TRUE`, arc width scales with filtered fragment support.
Junction label size is controlled with `junc_text_size`.

```{r arcs, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    junction_usage = "chr14:70234854-70234854",
    arc_height = 2,
    arc_side = "above",
    arc_scale = TRUE,
    junc_text_size = 2.5
)
```

## Sample colours and panel layout

The `colours` argument controls the colours used for sample coverage and
junction arcs.
It can be a single colour used for all samples or one colour per BAM file.

Axis text sizes can be adjusted with `axis_title_size` and `axis_text_size`.

```{r layout, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=7.5}
spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    annotation = annotation,
    colours = c("darkblue", "darkred"),
    panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1),
    axis_title_size = 20,
    axis_text_size = 12
)
```

## Returning and reusing plot data

Most users can work directly with the final plot returned by `spliceTerrain()`.
For advanced workflows, set `return_ctx = TRUE` to return the processed context
instead.
This contains validated settings, imported alignments, summarised coverage,
junction counts, annotation, and overlays.
The `gal` field contains one alignment object per sample: `GAlignments` for
single-end BAMs or `GAlignmentsList` for paired-end BAMs.
The paired-end list groups imported mates and includes mapped singleton reads.
The `cov` and `juncs` fields contain fragment summaries: `coverage_raw` holds
unnormalised fragment counts and `coverage` holds the plotting values after any
library-size normalisation.
The `juncs_all` field retains eligible junction summaries on the plotting
chromosome before display filtering or clipping, including out-of-window
junctions from imported alignments.
It provides a stable reference for the `usage_fraction` column in `juncs`.
That column is on the 0--1 scale, with `NA` for unselected junctions or an
undefined percentage.
All coordinate-bearing fields use genomic coordinates; compressed plot
coordinates are generated internally only when the context is plotted.

```{r return_ctx}
ctx <- spliceTerrain(
    bam = bams,
    region = region,
    annotation = annotation,
    min_junction_reads = 1,
    panel_heights = c(2, 2, 1),
    min_arrow = 100,
    return_ctx = TRUE
)

names(ctx)
```

The context can be passed back with the `ctx` argument to redraw the plot
without re-importing BAM files or recalculating coverage and junctions.
For example, the annotation can be used to retain only coverage overlapping
annotated exons and junctions that exactly match annotated introns.

```{r ctx_plot, fig.wide=TRUE, fig.height=6}
ctx$cov <- ctx$cov[overlapsAny(ctx$cov, ctx$annotation)]
ctx$juncs <- ctx$juncs[ctx$juncs$annotation_match]
spliceTerrain(ctx = ctx)
```

The `annotation_match` field records whether each junction exactly matches an
intron implied by the supplied annotation.
Plotting settings can also be changed directly, for example with
`ctx$colours <- c("darkblue", "darkred")`.
Settings that control BAM import, filtering, or normalisation are not reapplied
when a context is replotted because its coverage and junctions are already
processed.

Filtering `ctx$juncs` changes which arcs are displayed without changing the
usage denominator.
Changing `ctx$junction_usage` to another `GRanges` selection recalculates the
fractions from `ctx$juncs_all` when plotting.
If you intend to change the reference evidence itself, edit `ctx$juncs_all`,
retaining one row per sample/junction and non-negative `coverage_raw` counts.
The new argument names are `junction_usage` and `junction_usage_label_sep`.
They replace the development names `psi` and `psi_label_sep`.
Recreate older cached contexts with the current API.

# References

# Session information

```{r session_info}
sessionInfo() |>
    pander()
```
